## Task
You are a treasure hunter and found a pirate captain's diary. Read it carefully and pay close attention. Afterwards, trace the exact path the pirate took to hiding the treasure. Start at the last named location they visited before hiding the treasure and then follow the cardinal directions and distances. Use the following domain language to trace that path.

## Language to Trace the Path
This language is comprised of the following three actions to trace the pirate's path:
* StartAt(named location) to mark the beginning of the path at a named place.
* Sail(Miles, Direction) to mark movement along the path.
* Search() to indicate the end of the path and search the current place.

Make sure to wrap the actions in a triple backtick code block!
Keep sailing actions from different diary entries separate, even if two or more sailing actions go in the same direction.

## Named Locations
The following locations are named locations at which the path you should trace can start:
* Turtle Rock
* Treasure Island
* Monkey Island
* Devil's Spine
* King's Shore
* Widow's Cliff
* Whaler's Stranding
* Wicker's Basin
* St. John's Lagoon
* Half Moon Bay
* St. Anna's Harbor
* Barnacle Cove
* Fortune's Reach

## Example
Here is an example diary:

We arrived at Treasure Island.
-=-
Plundered the Shabby Lantern for their last 
rum and grain and took the ship out of the harbor 
before the guards could get reinforcements.
-=-
Sailed for some 50 miles North.

************************************************
Monday, October 16, 1724
************************************************
The crew is in good spirits this morning and 
is howling shanties at the moon.
-=- 
Continued our journey for another 30 miles North.
-=- 
Arrived at Monkey Island
************************************************

Left early and continued our journey. Sailed 
straight North, must have been 80 miles by
my reckoning.
-=-
Saw a huge swath of birds at one of the rock 
formations along the way, fascinating.
-=-
Covered another 20 miles North today, hardly 
a breeze around.

Sailed West for the entire day, covering 
about 150 miles.
-=-
Hid our treasure box at that islet with the 
three rock spikes.

Sailed North for around 20 miles before 
spotting some uncharted landmass to the East.

Your path:
```
StartAt(Monkey Island)
Sail(80, North)
Sail(20, North)
Sail(150, West)
Search()
```
## The Real Example

************************************************
Monday, September 24, 1703
************************************************
Grappled a fat merchantman. The iron sang and
the steel bit deep. Another prize for the tally.
-=-
The wind is blowing heavy from the East. We
happily accept the offer and go 90 miles with
the wind.
-=-
The bilge is a stagnant soup of rot. We bail or
we sink. The rhythm of the buckets is the
heartbeat of this ship.
-=-
Under tall dark clouds, we cut 80 miles South.
The men are crossing themselves.
************************************************

************************************************
Tuesday, September 25, 1703
************************************************
Brought her in to Widow's Cliff. This stretch of
coast is thick with smugglers and men who know
how to keep their mouths shut. We’ll trade what
we must and vanish into the blue again
-=-
The windlass is groaning as we weigh anchor.
Leaving Widow's Cliff behind to seek 40 miles
East, putting the stench of the docks in our
wake.
-=-
Stitching the black canvas myself. Every
puncture of the needle reminds me: we serve no
King but the wind.
-=-
Made it a mere 30 miles South in the past couple
hours.
-=-
Raided a coastal stead. Fresh grain and poultry
for the mess. The farmers' cries are a small
price for a full hold.
************************************************

************************************************
Wednesday, September 26, 1703
************************************************
We sailed for 20 miles South.
-=-
The holystones are out. If they have time to
complain, they have time to scrub the salt from
these boards until they gleam.
-=-
We sailed for 20 miles East.
-=-
Bent over the charts. The sea is a vast
graveyard, and only my compass keeps us from
joining the ghosts.
************************************************

************************************************
Thursday, September 27, 1703
************************************************
We sailed for 50 miles South.
-=-
Had five men on a rowboat set a marker 3 miles
West of here on a small island to lead the
greedy to a shallow grave. The real prize we
buried here in this sea cave. The high tide will
guard the entrance better than any man with a
pistol.
-=-
Spotted the royal colors to the North and made
off in the opposite direction immediately. We’ve
cut 100 miles, pushing the ship until the masts
groan, leaving the hunters to chase a shadow.
-=-
Slipping a weighted shroud into the deep. One
less mouth to feed, one more soul for Davy
Jones.
************************************************

************************************************
Friday, September 28, 1703
************************************************
We sailed for 70 miles South.
-=-
A pod of whales breached to starboard. A grand
omen, though the men only see a mountain of oil
and bone.
-=-
We sailed for 100 miles East.
-=-
The deck smells of goat dung and salt. A
nuisance, but the fresh milk is the only thing
keeping the fever at bay.
************************************************

************************************************
Saturday, September 29, 1703
************************************************
Strained every inch of canvas to cover 40 miles
South. We are a ghost on the water.
-=-
The men are howling shanties. A rough choir of
rogues, but they find the beat well enough.
-=-
Sudden heavy wind from the North pushed us 20
miles downwind through mist and spray that stung
the eyes and salted the soul.
-=-
I feel their eyes on my back. A low murmur in
the galley that stops when I pass. Let them
whisper; my pistol is loaded.
************************************************

************************************************
Sunday, September 30, 1703
************************************************
The gale took us in its teeth, dragging the ship
80 miles South against every effort of the crew.
We are at the mercy of the gods now.
-=-
Reached Half Moon Bay with a battered hull. We
require timber and fresh water, and this
settlement is the only place to find them. As
soon as the seams are pitched, we’re back to
sea—every hour at the dock is an hour closer to
the gallows.
-=-
Leaving Half Moon Bay to the rats and the tax-
men. We are heading East for 20 miles, seeking
better fortune and cleaner water than this port
could offer.
-=-
Dice rattling below deck. I'll let them play for
now—better they lose their coin to each other
than their tempers to me.
************************************************

************************************************
Monday, October 01, 1703
************************************************
Spotted the royal colors to the North and made
off in the opposite direction immediately. We’ve
cut 30 miles, pushing the ship until the masts
groan, leaving the hunters to chase a shadow.
-=-
Hands black with tar today. The rigging is
stayed and coated; I'll not have a line snap
when the heavens open up.
-=-
We sailed for 50 miles East.
-=-
The men are spinning yarns of sea-serpents
again. Foolishness.
************************************************

************************************************
Tuesday, October 02, 1703
************************************************
We sailed for 40 miles East.
-=-
She’s taking on water in the hold. We’ve plugged
the seams with oakum and prayer. She’ll hold...
for now.
-=-
Heading East with a following wind, we sailed
for 100 miles. Every mile brings us closer to
the prize or the noose.
-=-
Put into Wicker's Basin to bleed the prize money
and fill the hold. A weary town for a weary
crew, but the gold spends just as well here.
We’ll take on flour and shot, then clear the bay
before the harbor master can draft his report.
************************************************

************************************************
Wednesday, October 03, 1703
************************************************
Cleared the harbor. I've set the watch and laid
a course for 30 North. The business of the shore
is done; the business of the sea begins.
-=-
Haggling with a fence in a hidden cove. He takes
a shark's share of the prize, but gold is
lighter than a hold full of stolen sugar.
-=-
The sea turned to glass. We drifted a mere 30
miles East, the men cursing the idle sails.
************************************************
Note: This diary belongs to Dry-Ink Dirk of whom is known that his logs are nothing but the truth.
Now, chart your path, treasure hunter!
